title: Shantanu and Ganga
hook: seven sons are given to the river while a king keeps his vow of silence; at the eighth, he speaks
carry: the riverbank isn't the whole story

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pratipa's riddle, and the vow never to stop or question her. Did you read the terms before you said yes? Day seven hundred six.

A son is born to the king and queen. And the queen carries the baby down to the river, and gives him to the Ganga's waters. As she does it, she says it's for his good. Shantanu watches from the bank, and says nothing. He remembers what he promised: never stop her, never speak harshly to her, or she leaves. Another son is born, and the same thing happens. And another. The text tells it plainly, without looking away.
screen: `A SON IS BORN.` → `GIVEN TO THE RIVER.` → `THE KING SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Seven sons, the text says, one after another, into the river. And Shantanu, every time, stays silent, because he's afraid that if he speaks, she'll leave him. Then the eighth son is born. As she carries this one toward the river, Shantanu can't hold it in. He speaks. Don't kill him, he says. Who are you? Why do you kill your own sons? She stops. I won't kill this one, she says. But my time with you is over, as we agreed. And she tells him who she is: Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu, the text says. The sons, she explains, were the Vasus, cursed to be born as men, and she has freed them as she promised. Now hear it from where we stand. Two days ago we heard the Vasus beg for this. Yesterday we watched the vow get made. Today we see what it cost, and the scene can be seen three ways. For Shantanu, these were his children, lost in front of him. For the Vasus, it was the release they asked for. For Ganga, it was a promise kept to the letter. The Mahabharata doesn't smooth this over. It lets the scene stay hard. Some readers take it as a story about curses and karma working themselves out. Some hear it as a picture of what an unquestioning vow can cost. Some take from it that what's seen from the riverbank isn't the whole story. And the son who lives carries the Vasus' power, and their word that he'll have no children. Ganga takes the child with her, and goes.
screen: `SEVEN SONS, AND SILENCE.` · `AT THE EIGHTH, HE SPEAKS.` · `I AM GANGA, DAUGHTER OF JAHNU.` · `THREE VIEWS OF ONE SCENE.` · then, large: `THE RIVERBANK ISN'T THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: This is a hard story, so go gently. Let the breath settle. Bring to mind something you once watched happen and didn't understand, something that looked only like loss. You don't have to find a hidden meaning in it. Some things stay hard. Just let it be seen, and breathe beside it. If there's a part you now see differently, notice that too. The bell holds the time.
Vasus. The gods cursed to be born as men, given to the river seven times, and spared the eighth when the king finally spoke.
Your line: the riverbank isn't the whole story. Today, when you can see only part of something, say so, out loud or to yourself. Day seven hundred six.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families carry the ashes of their dead to the Ganga, at places such as Haridwar and Varanasi, trusting the river as Ganga is trusted in this story: as a mother whose waters release.

pairs: daughter of Jahnu, the text says

myth: Shantanu objected to the very first drowning
he stayed silent seven times, afraid she'd leave.
she spared the eighth son and left, as they'd agreed.
the drowned sons were the Vasus
gods cursed to be born as men, whom she freed as she'd promised.

fork.setup: you're Shantanu. your wife carries your eighth son to the river. you promised never to stop her. what do you do?
options: speak up and ask her to stop.
fork.reveal: he speaks. she spares the child, names herself Ganga, and leaves, as their agreement said she would.

original.note: Sanskrit vasu: the Vasus are a group of gods; here, the sons Ganga freed in her waters.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mother who drowns her children.
what it means: a goddess keeping a promise to gods who begged for release, seen through a father's eyes.
what a scholar hears: Ganga names herself daughter of Jahnu, and the spared eighth son carries the Vasus' power.
recall: touched with the tops of the grass

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Ganga's sons given to the river; Shantanu speaks at the eighth; Ganga reveals herself)

notes: All paraphrase. Seven sons drowned and the eighth spared are the text's numbers; confirm in Ganguli.
Ganga's words at each drowning are paraphrased as 'for his good'; confirm.
Ganga calls herself daughter of Jahnu in this passage; confirm.
The three 'some readers' takes are unattributed interpretations, given without ranking; a Keeper may wish to adjust them.
The account of Vasishtha's cow and Devavrata's return is left for the following days, which carry the same title.

Editor (y3 audit): Ganga names herself only 'daughter of Jahnu' (cut 'the sage'); the three views are now the script's framing, not attributed to the poem; replaced unsourced claims about reciters and children's retellings in howItsDone with a line from the text's order; varied the practice opener and cut a repeated 'if you pray' line.

Editor (y3 re-audit): howItsDone described the story's order instead of anything people do, and repeated for a third day the point that the listener knows what Shantanu doesn't; replaced with the custom of carrying ashes to the Ganga. Confirm the phrasing of the custom.
